title: Accessibility
scopeHtml: Scope: Compose semantics, TalkBack behavior, touch targets, font scaling, Views vs Compose accessibility, testing, RTL/localization. Versions marked "verify" were not confirmed against release notes.

questions.promptHtml: What is the semantics tree in Compose, and how does it relate to the composition and what TalkBack sees?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know accessibility in Compose is a parallel data structure, not "set contentDescription on views".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Alongside the UI node tree, Compose builds a semantics tree. Each node carries properties like text, role, state, actions. AndroidComposeView exposes it to the platform as an AccessibilityNodeInfo hierarchy through an accessibility delegate, so TalkBack, Switch Access and Voice Access read semantics, not pixels. Material components set sensible semantics by default; custom drawing and gestures need me to add them.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Semantics are attached via Modifier.semantics { }. Built-ins (Text, Button, clickable, toggleable) add their own through the same modifier.
  • There are two views of the tree: the merged tree (what accessibility services see, children folded into a parent that has mergeDescendants = true, as clickable does) and the unmerged tree (every node, what tests can opt into with useUnmergedTree = true).
  • Compose does not create real Views per node. The platform needs AccessibilityNodeInfo objects, so a delegate creates virtual nodes on demand when an accessibility service is enabled and sends events when semantics change.
  • Semantics are independent from drawing: a Canvas that draws a chart has an empty semantics node until you describe it.
Composition  --> LayoutNodes --> SemanticsNodes (unmerged)
                                      | merge rules (mergeDescendants)
                                      v
                              merged tree --> AccessibilityNodeInfo --> TalkBack

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Box(
    Modifier
        .size(120.dp)
        .semantics {
            contentDescription = "Sales chart, up 12 percent this week"
            role = Role.Image
        }
) { MyCanvasChart() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming a custom-drawn component is "accessible because it is visible".
  • Debugging only the unmerged tree; TalkBack sees the merged one.
  • Thinking semantics cost nothing: a delegate only does real work when a service is on, but huge unmerged trees still hurt.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do tests read semantics from? → SemanticsNodeInteraction; merged tree by default, unmerged with useUnmergedTree.
  2. How do you inspect it? → Layout Inspector semantics view, printToLog("TAG") in tests, Accessibility Scanner.
  3. When is the delegate active? → Only when an accessibility service (or UI Automator style tooling) is enabled; it is lazily populated.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "semantics is how Compose does contentDescription". Senior: merged vs unmerged trees, virtual node delegate, semantics independent from draw, and that custom components own their semantics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A canvas-based chart shipped with zero semantics; TalkBack users heard nothing for the main screen element until a review flagged it.

questions.promptHtml: When should an Icon or Image have a contentDescription, and when should it be null? What makes a good description?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common review finding; checks judgment, not syntax.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: If the image conveys information or is the only label of an action, describe what it means or does, not what it looks like. If it is decorative or redundant with adjacent text, pass null so TalkBack skips it. Do not include the role ("button") because the role is announced separately, and localize the string.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Icon(contentDescription: String?) and Image(...) take it as a required parameter so you must decide. null means "no semantics node content", not "forgot".
  • Inside an IconButton, the button needs the description, not a sibling Text. For a Button(onClick) { Icon(...); Text("Save") } the icon is redundant, so null; the merged button reads "Save".
  • Describe function: "Add to cart" not "Plus icon". For state, prefer stateDescription over rewriting the description.
  • Avoid concatenating the visible label again, and avoid trailing "image" or "button".
  • Strings come from stringResource; hardcoded English breaks localized TalkBack users.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Informative action: the icon is the only label.
IconButton(onClick = onShare) {
    Icon(Icons.Default.Share, contentDescription = stringResource(R.string.share))
}
// Decorative next to text: null.
Row {
    Icon(Icons.Default.Star, contentDescription = null)
    Text(stringResource(R.string.favorites))
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Describing appearance ("blue circle") instead of purpose.
  • Putting contentDescription on a Text; it overrides the text for services, hiding the real content (use it only when the visible text is truly unclear).
  • Empty string instead of null on a clickable icon: the test framework flags it and TalkBack reads "unlabeled".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Image loaded from the network, user-generated? → Describe if you have alt text from the backend; otherwise mark decorative or ask product for alt text; never fabricate.
  2. Dynamic content like a rating? → "Rated 4 out of 5 stars" built from the value, with plurals.
  3. Does null remove the node from the tree? → The icon contributes no description; whether a node exists depends on other semantics. Use clearAndSetSemantics or hideFromAccessibility (verify version) to truly remove.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE adds descriptions everywhere. Senior distinguishes informative / decorative / functional images, avoids duplicates, localizes, and gets alt text for user content from the API.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A product grid read "image, image, image" 40 times because thumbnails had a description equal to the file name.

questions.promptHtml: Explain mergeDescendants, clearAndSetSemantics and hiding from accessibility. When do you use each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Card/list rows are where Compose accessibility goes wrong; this shows control of the tree.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: mergeDescendants = true folds child nodes into one focusable node whose text is the concatenation, which is right for a card that acts as one unit. clearAndSetSemantics throws away the children's semantics and replaces them with what I write, for when I want a single crafted announcement. For purely decorative content I hide it from accessibility. clickable, toggleable and selectable already merge.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Without merging every Text is a separate TalkBack stop: a row with title, subtitle, price and a "Buy" icon is 4+ swipes, and the user hears no grouping.
  • Modifier.semantics(mergeDescendants = true) {} merges children into this node. Child properties combine per each property's merge policy (text lists concatenate; some, like traversalIndex, never merge).
  • A merged node containing clickable children: the parent's click becomes the primary; child actions that must stay separately reachable need to live outside the merged node or be exposed as custom actions (see Q331).
  • clearAndSetSemantics { contentDescription = "..." } replaces the subtree's semantics. Use it when the concatenation sounds wrong ("$ 4 99 per month" read as parts). It removes child actions too, so re-add them.
  • Hiding: Modifier.semantics { hideFromAccessibility() } (newer API; verify the Compose version, older code used invisibleToUser()) keeps semantics for tests while hiding from services.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Row(
    Modifier
        .semantics(mergeDescendants = true) {}
        .clickable(onClick = onOpen)
) {
    Text(item.title); Text(item.subtitle)
}

Row(
    Modifier.clearAndSetSemantics {
        contentDescription = "${item.title}, ${item.priceSpoken}"
        onClick(label = "Open details") { onOpen(); true }
    }
) { /* visual price formatting that would be read badly */ }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• clearAndSetSemantics wiping a child button's action so it becomes unreachable.
  • Merging a whole screen section, hiding independent controls.
  • Forgetting tests use the merged tree: onNodeWithText("Buy") fails after merging; use useUnmergedTree = true.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does clickable merge? → Yes, it sets merging on its node.
  2. Hidden decorative element and tests? → Hide-from-accessibility keeps it in the tree for tests; clearAndSetSemantics on a leaf does not.
  3. Two buttons inside a clickable card? → Keep the card clickable, expose the buttons as customActions or restructure so buttons are siblings outside the merged node.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows "merge to group". Senior reasons about what is lost on merge/clear (child actions), merge policies, and test implications.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After wrapping product cards in clearAndSetSemantics, the wishlist heart inside became unreachable for TalkBack users; a support ticket, not a test, caught it.

questions.promptHtml: How do you make a custom toggle, tab or checkbox announce correctly in TalkBack? What are Role, stateDescription and the onClick label for?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Custom controls built from Box + clickable are the usual source of "unknown element" announcements.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: TalkBack announces name, role, state, then the available action. I use Modifier.toggleable/selectable/clickable(role = ...) so the role and checked state are set for me; stateDescription for custom state text like "Expanded"; and an action label so the hint says "double tap to open settings", not just "double tap to activate".

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Role values: Button, Checkbox, Switch, RadioButton, Tab, Image, DropdownList. TalkBack maps them to localized words.
  • toggleable(value, role = Role.Switch, onValueChange) sets toggleableState plus click action; the platform announces "on/off".
  • stateDescription overrides the spoken state for cases the built-ins cannot express (e.g. "3 of 5 steps complete").
  • clickable(onClickLabel = "...") or semantics { onClick(label) } customizes the action hint. Same for onLongClickLabel.
  • Disabled: enabled = false is exposed; prefer that over opacity-only visuals.
  • Headings: semantics { heading() } lets users jump heading to heading.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Row(
    Modifier
        .toggleable(
            value = checked,
            role = Role.Switch,
            onValueChange = onChange
        )
        .semantics { stateDescription = if (checked) "Notifications on" else "Notifications off" }
) {
    Text("Notifications")
    Switch(checked = checked, onCheckedChange = null) // visual only; row owns the semantics
}
Text("Account", Modifier.semantics { heading() })

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Switch inside a clickable row with both handling clicks: two focus stops and double toggles. Pass onCheckedChange = null and let the row own it.
  • Conveying state by color only.
  • Overriding stateDescription with static text that goes stale.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why role matters for Switch Access / Voice Access? → Services use role and actions to offer commands like "click Notifications".
  2. Tabs? → selectable(role = Role.Tab) inside a tab row; Material Tab does it.
  3. Progress? → progressBarRangeInfo/ProgressBarRangeInfo so value is announced, not just drawn.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE adds contentDescription "toggle". Senior uses the semantic primitives (role, toggleable state, action labels, headings) so all services, not only TalkBack, work.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A custom chip filter read "button" with no selected state; blind users could not tell which filters were active.

questions.contextHtml: Your design team ships a dense "compact" list for a trading-style app: 24dp close icons, 32dp chips, rows 40dp high, to fit 14 rows per screen instead of 9. Accessibility Scanner flags 2,300 "touch target too small" findings across 31 screens. Product says density drives retention (A/B: +6% session length for compact). Support logs show 4% of mis-taps on the close icon, double the app average. The Material components in use already enforce a minimum, but several custom Box(Modifier.size(24.dp).clickable{}) do not.
questions.promptHtml: How do you resolve density vs touch target requirements?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make everything 48dp." That throws away the A/B win and ignores that the visual size and the hit area are separable. Or the opposite: "Scanner warnings are advisory, ship it."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is 48dp a legal requirement for our markets (WCAG 2.2 target size minimum is 24 CSS px, enhanced is 44; Android guidance is 48dp; verify the contract wording)? Which targets are primary vs rare? Are targets spaced apart (spacing can offset small size)? What do mis-tap analytics say per control?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the highest-mis-tap controls (close icon) first; do not wait for a redesign.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) custom clickables skipping Material's minimum enforcement; (b) designs conflating visual size with hit size; (c) tightly packed neighbors making overlap; (d) text-heavy rows only need row-level tap, not per-element.
  4. How I'd verify: Layout Inspector bounds, Accessibility Scanner, assertTouchHeightIsEqualTo(48.dp) / assertTouchWidthIsEqualTo in Compose tests (they measure touch bounds, not drawn bounds).
  5. Root cause: Hit area follows the clickable's layout bounds. Material 3 wraps interactive components with minimumInteractiveComponentSize() (48dp by default; the local is LocalMinimumInteractiveComponentSize, naming varies by version, verify) which pads the touch area without enlarging visuals. Custom Box.size(24.dp).clickable bypasses it.
  6. Fix: Keep the 24dp icon visually, enlarge the target:
Box(
    Modifier
        .minimumInteractiveComponentSize() // 48dp touch area, 24dp visual stays inside
        .clickable(role = Role.Button, onClickLabel = "Close", onClick = onClose),
    contentAlignment = Alignment.Center
) { Icon(Icons.Default.Close, contentDescription = null, Modifier.size(24.dp)) }

Make the whole row clickable and drop per-element targets where possible. Ensure neighboring 48dp areas do not overlap awkwardly (overlap resolves to z-order). 7. Prevention: Lint/Detekt rule banning raw clickable on sub-48dp boxes; a shared AppIconButton; a test helper asserting touch size on screens. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not shrink LocalMinimumInteractiveComponentSize globally to hit density numbers; that disables the safety net for the whole app. A user-facing "compact mode" toggle is acceptable only if default stays compliant.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two adjacent icons 24dp apart, 48dp targets would overlap → Increase spacing, or merge into an overflow menu; overlapped targets mis-tap more than small ones.
  • Does bigger target hurt visuals? → No, padding is invisible; ripple bounds can look larger, so clip ripple with indication bounded if needed.
  • Does a11y service ever bypass size? → Switch Access and TalkBack focus the node regardless of size, but low-vision and motor-impaired touch users depend on it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team "fixed" 400 scanner warnings with a global minimum override then discovered ripple halos overlapping in a toolbar; the real fix was a single AppIconButton and removing a dozen raw clickables.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Treats warnings as noise or inflates every visual to 48dp.
  • Hire: Separates visual and hit size, uses minimum interactive component.
  • Strong hire: Adds measurable tests, spacing reasoning, analytics-driven prioritization, and the design-system guardrail.

questions.contextHtml:
A settings screen passes design review visually. In the accessibility audit, TalkBack users report: each row needs 3 swipes, toggling announces "unlabeled, button" and toggling sometimes fires twice. Code:

@Composable
fun SettingRow(title: String, desc: String, checked: Boolean, onChange: (Boolean) -> Unit) {
    Row(
        Modifier
            .fillMaxWidth()
            .clickable { onChange(!checked) }
            .padding(16.dp)
    ) {
        Column(Modifier.weight(1f)) {
            Text(title)
            Text(desc, color = Color.Gray)
        }
        Switch(checked = checked, onCheckedChange = onChange)
        Icon(Icons.Default.Info, contentDescription = "")
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find the accessibility defects and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add contentDescription to the Switch." Misses the duplicated click, the focus stops and the empty description.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should the info icon be interactive? Is the whole row the toggle target (it is by the clickable)? Which TalkBack and Compose version?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an outage; ship a targeted fix in the next release, with the row component shared.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked / defects: (a) Row has clickable and Switch also handles clicks: two nodes with actions; the clickable merges descendants but the Switch's own action/state is still exposed and onChange(!checked) plus the switch's own callback can both fire; (b) clickable is a plain click, so no Role.Switch or checked state; (c) the info icon has contentDescription = "", flagged as unlabeled; it is decorative so should be null (or interactive and labeled); (d) tap target of Switch plus row padding fine, but focus order has multiple stops.
  4. How I'd verify: Compose test with printToLog merged and unmerged; TalkBack swipe count; enable enableAccessibilityChecks() (Compose 1.8+, see Q332).
  5. Root cause: The row's semantics describe a generic click while the switch owns the real state; two interactive owners for one setting.
  6. Fix:
Row(
    Modifier
        .fillMaxWidth()
        .toggleable(value = checked, role = Role.Switch, onValueChange = onChange)
        .padding(16.dp)
) {
    Column(Modifier.weight(1f)) { Text(title); Text(desc, color = Color.Gray) }
    Switch(checked = checked, onCheckedChange = null) // visual only
    Icon(Icons.Default.Info, contentDescription = null)
}

TalkBack now reads "title, desc, switch, on. Double tap to toggle" as a single stop. Gray text also needs a contrast check (see Q333). 7. Prevention: A shared SettingToggleRow in the design system; a Compose test asserting isToggleable() and a single node. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add clearAndSetSemantics with a hand-built string; it duplicates state and rots when the title changes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The info icon must open a help sheet → Keep it outside the toggleable row as a sibling with its own label and 48dp target, or expose it as a custom action.
  • Why can the switch toggle twice? → Row click and switch click both call onChange with different values captured at different times.
  • Why gray text matters → Contrast ratio below 4.5:1 for normal text fails WCAG AA.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A row component copied into 60 call sites carried this bug; fixing it once in the shared composable closed 60 findings in the next audit.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds descriptions only.
  • Hire: Moves ownership to toggleable, nulls the switch callback, fixes the icon.
  • Strong hire: Explains merge/click semantics, tests it, shares the component.

questions.promptHtml: How do font scale and display size affect a Compose layout, and how do you build UI that survives 200% text?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Clipped text at large font scale is a top accessibility regression and a classic layout-quality signal.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Text in sp scales with the user's font-size setting; dp scales with display size. Since Android 14 scaling is nonlinear (large text grows less than small text) and goes up to 200% (verify OEM variance). So I never fix heights on text containers, allow wrapping and minHeight, stack rows vertically when space runs out, and test at 200% font and largest display size.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• LocalDensity.current.fontScale exposes the factor; sp converts via it. Display size changes density itself, shrinking available dp width.
  • Fixed height(48.dp) on a button with a long label clips at 2x; use heightIn(min = 48.dp).
  • Text scale also affects Text maxLines and ellipsis: truncating essential info (price, error) is a defect. Allow wrapping or scroll.
  • Responsive reflow: BoxWithConstraints/FlowRow, or switch Row to Column when fontScale > 1.3f. Use sparingly; prefer layouts that reflow naturally.
  • Do not cap text with LocalDensity provides Density(density, fontScale = 1f) to "fix" layout; it ignores the user's need. Cap only for specific constrained UI (e.g. bottom-bar labels) and still keep within a sane maximum.
  • Android 14 nonlinear scaling reduces extreme enlargement on already-large text, so tests should still hit the max.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun PriceRow(label: String, price: String) {
    val big = LocalDensity.current.fontScale > 1.3f
    if (big) Column { Text(label); Text(price, style = MaterialTheme.typography.titleLarge) }
    else Row(Modifier.fillMaxWidth(), horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.SpaceBetween) {
        Text(label); Text(price, style = MaterialTheme.typography.titleLarge)
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using dp for font sizes or sp for icon sizes tied to text.
  • Fixed-height cards and bottom bars clipping.
  • Testing only at 1.0 and 1.3; the failures appear at 1.5+ and combined with largest display size.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Previews? → @PreviewFontScale and @PreviewScreenSizes (verify availability) to render many scales at once.
  2. Min text size? → Material type scale in sp; avoid below 12sp for content.
  3. Does the user get a different density by "Display size"? → Yes, densityDpi changes; a 360dp-wide phone can become ~320dp, triggering narrower layouts.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "use sp". Senior knows the two independent settings, nonlinear scale, reflow strategies, min-height rule and automated screenshot tests at multiple scales.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout "Pay" button clipped its amount at 200% font; conversion dropped for a segment older users before anyone linked it to font scale.

questions.promptHtml: How does TalkBack decide focus order in Compose, and how do you fix a wrong reading order?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Reading order bugs appear in overlays, FABs and cards with scattered layouts.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The default is layout order: top to bottom, then left to right (start to end), derived from bounds, not composition order. When that is wrong I group related items with isTraversalGroup = true on a parent and order children with traversalIndex (lower reads first, can be negative). I avoid reordering the code just to fix reading order.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Without hints, the platform sorts semantic nodes by position; a FAB drawn in a Box after content is read last even if visually prominent.
  • isTraversalGroup makes the subtree a unit: TalkBack finishes the group before moving on. traversalIndex is a Float on children, compared within the group, and never merges with parent values.
  • A parent with a traversal group should also reflect logical structure: a card is one group, so title and price are not interleaved with a neighbor card in a two-column grid.
  • Not every change needs this: fix layout when the structure itself is misleading.
  • Legacy Views equivalents: accessibilityTraversalBefore/After (API 22+) and importantForAccessibility.
  • Focus handling for keyboards/D-pad is a separate system (focusable, FocusRequester), though both should agree.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Box(Modifier.semantics { isTraversalGroup = true }) {
    FloatingActionButton(
        onClick = onAdd,
        modifier = Modifier.semantics { traversalIndex = -1f } // read first
    ) { Icon(Icons.Default.Add, contentDescription = "Add task") }
    TaskList()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Setting traversalIndex without a traversal group on the parent, producing partial or surprising order.
  • Using zIndex to influence reading order; it only affects drawing and touch.
  • Absolute index numbers copied across screens; indexes are relative within a group.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Two-column grid reads row by row mixing columns? → Make each card a group (or merge) so each reads in full.
  2. Dialog and background? → Dialog windows get focus; ensure paneTitle and that background is not focusable (modal).
  3. How to check? → TalkBack linear swipe, Layout Inspector semantics, Accessibility Scanner.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE reorders composables. Senior uses traversal semantics, understands bounds-based default sort and keeps keyboard focus consistent.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A bottom sheet's "Confirm" read before its title because it was positioned by offset; blind users confirmed purchases without hearing the amount.

questions.promptHtml: How does accessibility differ between the View system and Compose? What do you do differently when migrating?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks you can carry accessibility through a mixed codebase.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Views expose AccessibilityNodeInfo directly: android:contentDescription, importantForAccessibility, labelFor, AccessibilityDelegateCompat for customizing, accessibilityLiveRegion. Compose builds a semantics tree and a delegate generates the virtual nodes, so I use Modifier.semantics. Standard widgets are accessible in both; custom views and custom composables are on me. In migration I port the delegate logic to semantics and retest.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Concern Views Compose
Label contentDescription, labelFor contentDescription, Text merges
Custom actions ViewCompat.addAccessibilityAction, delegate semantics { customActions = ... }
Skip decorative importantForAccessibility="no" contentDescription = null, hide-from-accessibility
Order traversalBefore/After isTraversalGroup, traversalIndex
Live region accessibilityLiveRegion liveRegion = LiveRegionMode.Polite
Custom drawn virtual children ExploreByTouchHelper semantics on child composables
Role AccessibilityNodeInfo.className, roleDescription Role
  • Interop: AndroidView content keeps its native a11y; ComposeView content merges into the host window's tree.
  • Compose touch target enforcement is built into Material; Views need minHeight/TouchDelegate.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Migrating a custom View with an AccessibilityDelegate and dropping it silently.
  • importantForAccessibility mistakes on View containers that hide children.
  • Assuming a ComposeView gets no a11y focus order integration; it does, via its own delegate.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. TouchDelegate? → Enlarges a View's touch area to a parent-defined rect; Compose uses minimum interactive size.
  2. ExploreByTouchHelper? → Provides virtual nodes for custom-drawn Views; in Compose just add semantics.
  3. How do you announce something in Views? → announceForAccessibility (limited; prefer live regions).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists attributes. Senior maps each Views construct to its semantics counterpart and audits custom delegates during migration.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After migrating a seat-map custom View to Compose Canvas, seat selection became silent because the ExploreByTouchHelper was dropped without replacement.

questions.promptHtml: How do you tell TalkBack about dynamic content changes (errors, toasts, counters) in Compose, and what are the failure modes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Dynamic UI is where visual-only feedback leaves blind users without information.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I mark the changing element with liveRegion = LiveRegionMode.Polite so TalkBack announces content changes without moving focus; Assertive interrupts and is for urgent errors only. For one-off messages I rely on Snackbar/AccessibilityManager announcements rather than ad hoc announce calls, and I never put a live region on something that changes every second.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• A live region node sends TYPE_WINDOW_CONTENT_CHANGED with CONTENT_CHANGE_TYPE_TEXT when its text changes; TalkBack speaks the node's text (or description).
  • Polite queues after current speech; Assertive interrupts. Overuse floods users and drowns real focus feedback.
  • Scope: place the live region on the node whose text is the message, not a large container, or it re-reads everything.
  • Error handling in forms: also set the field's error semantics (semantics { error("Invalid email") }) and move focus to the first invalid field.
  • Page/screen changes: paneTitle semantic announces when a pane (dialog, bottom sheet, screen) appears.
  • Snackbar from Material has live-region behavior by default; custom toasts often have none.
  • Transient visuals (a 2s toast) disappear before slow readers finish, so persist important errors in layout.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Text(
    text = errorMessage,
    modifier = Modifier.semantics { liveRegion = LiveRegionMode.Polite },
    color = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.error
)
// Screen/pane title:
Surface(Modifier.semantics { paneTitle = "Checkout" }) { /* ... */ }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Live region on a ticking timer or progress percentage (see Q336).
  • Relying on color change to show an error.
  • Announcing success then immediately moving focus, cutting the announcement.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Polite vs Assertive? → Polite waits; assertive interrupts, errors only.
  2. When does a live region not fire? → If text does not actually change or the node is not in the tree yet when state is set; the node must exist before updating.
  3. Can you announce without a node? → Views have announceForAccessibility (deprecated in recent API levels; verify), Compose should use live regions or Snackbar.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE adds liveRegion everywhere. Senior limits scope and frequency, pairs with error semantics and focus movement, and considers persistence of messages.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A login error appeared visually only; TalkBack users believed the button did nothing after a failed attempt.

questions.contextHtml: Product wants a messaging inbox with swipe-to-archive and swipe-to-delete, plus a long-press menu. 11% of your 1.8M DAU use some assistive technology (TalkBack, Switch Access, Voice Access, large font) according to a recent survey (illustrative). The requirement doc says only: "Support swipe actions on rows". Early build: SwipeToDismissBox rows; TalkBack users report they cannot archive; Switch Access users cannot reach the delete action at all. Each row also contains a "reply" button.
questions.promptHtml: How do you deliver the feature accessibly with a vague requirement?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add contentDescription to the row" or "tell users to use two-finger swipe"; gestures are not discoverable and many services do not synthesize swipes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must swipe be the only path, or can archive/delete exist elsewhere (detail screen)? Is delete reversible (undo)? Which services does support need to cover? Is the reply button a separate action?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add an overflow menu or detail-screen archive/delete as a non-gesture path before launch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) swipe gesture invisible to services; (b) merged row hides inner button; (c) delete lacks confirmation or undo.
  4. How I'd verify: TalkBack with the local context menu (actions menu), Switch Access scan, Voice Access "show actions".
  5. Root cause: Gesture-only actions have no semantic action. Semantics customActions surface actions in TalkBack's actions menu and Switch Access.
  6. Fix:
Row(
    Modifier
        .semantics(mergeDescendants = true) {
            customActions = listOf(
                CustomAccessibilityAction("Archive") { onArchive(); true },
                CustomAccessibilityAction("Delete") { onDelete(); true },
                CustomAccessibilityAction("Reply") { onReply(); true },
            )
        }
        .clickable(onClick = onOpen)
) { /* ... */ }

Keep a visible, tappable reply button for sighted users but expose it as a custom action in the merged row so the row remains one stop. Keep swipe for sighted users. Announce the result (Snackbar with Undo). 7. Prevention: A design-system rule: every gesture needs a non-gesture equivalent; a test asserting SemanticsProperties.CustomActions on gesture rows. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make the action the only way or put 3 always-visible buttons that eat 48dp each of density; customActions keep the UI clean.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Voice Access says "click archive" fails → Voice Access can show actions on request; make labels short, unique and verbs.
  • Action label localization → Use string resources; labels are spoken.
  • Same for long-press? → Yes: expose via onLongClick label or custom action.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A feed shipped swipe actions only; accessibility feedback arrived in a store review with a one-line fix of adding customActions that cost 20 lines.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests gesture instructions or only labels.
  • Hire: Uses customActions and a non-gesture path.
  • Strong hire: Handles merge trade-offs, undo, tests and design rule.

questions.promptHtml: How do you test accessibility on Android, automated and manual, for Compose and Views?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Teams that only run manual TalkBack passes regress every release; this checks tooling literacy.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Layers: lint and Compose UI Check in previews for early signals; Accessibility Test Framework checks in instrumented tests (Compose 1.8+: enableAccessibilityChecks(); Espresso: AccessibilityChecks.enable()); semantics assertions for behavior; Accessibility Scanner and manual TalkBack, Switch Access and large-font passes for what automation cannot judge.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Compose semantics tests: onNodeWithContentDescription, assertContentDescriptionEquals, assertHasClickAction, isToggleable, assert(SemanticsMatcher.expectValue(SemanticsProperties.Role, Role.Switch)), onRoot().printToLog("A11Y"), useUnmergedTree = true to see children.
  • Compose accessibility checks (Compose 1.8.0+ per docs): add androidx.compose.ui:ui-test-junit4-accessibility, call composeTestRule.enableAccessibilityChecks(); checks run on actions or by tryPerformAccessibilityChecks(). Based on the Accessibility Test Framework (same base as Accessibility Scanner). Third-party notes suggest it needs API 34+ (verify).
  • It catches: missing labels, small touch targets, low contrast (some), duplicate click bounds. It cannot judge reading order quality, meaningfulness of labels, or focus flow.
  • Manual: TalkBack swipe through every screen, check heading navigation, reading order, dialogs and error flows; Switch Access; font 200% and display size largest; keyboard navigation.
  • CI: screenshot tests at font scales and RTL; fail builds on new scanner violations with a baseline.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@get:Rule val rule = createAndroidComposeRule<MainActivity>()

@Test fun checkoutIsAccessible() {
    rule.enableAccessibilityChecks()
    rule.onNodeWithText("Pay").assertHasClickAction().performClick()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating a green scanner as "accessible"; automated tools find roughly the mechanical subset.
  • Tests using merged tree and missing child issues.
  • Only testing default font scale.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Suppress known issues? → Configure the validator with result filters/baselines; track them as debt.
  2. Where do previews fit? → Compose UI Check mode in Android Studio audits previews (verify version).
  3. Do you test with real users? → Yes, periodic sessions with assistive-technology users; best signal.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE runs Accessibility Scanner once. Senior wires automated checks into CI with baselines, adds semantics assertions to feature tests and defines a manual checklist per release.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A release passed all unit tests but failed audit because no test ever enabled accessibility checks; one line caught 40 violations.

questions.contextHtml: Two weeks before an enterprise launch, a customer's third-party audit against WCAG 2.1 AA fails your Android app with 87 findings in 5 categories: 31 missing/empty labels, 22 contrast failures (gray hint text at 2.6:1, brand-orange buttons with white text at 3.1:1), 14 touch targets under 48dp, 12 reading-order issues, 8 focus traps in custom dialogs. Contract penalty applies if not fixed by launch. The team has 6 Android devs, a Compose/Views mixed codebase, and one designer.
questions.promptHtml: How do you triage, fix and prevent recurrence?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Fixing all 87 one by one in screen order, with no root-cause grouping, and no regression protection.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which WCAG level and which criteria are contractual? Which flows does the customer actually use (login, core task)? Is the brand color change allowed? What device/TalkBack versions did the auditor use?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Triage by user impact: blockers (focus traps, unlabeled primary actions) first, because they make flows impossible; contrast and sizes next.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (clustering root causes): Findings collapse into maybe 8 causes: a handful of design-system components (button, text field, dialog), the theme's color tokens, and a shared row.
  4. How I'd verify: Accessibility Scanner per screen, Compose accessibility checks in tests, manual TalkBack on the critical flows, contrast calculator.
  5. Root cause: No accessibility acceptance criteria in definition-of-done; custom components bypassed Material defaults; palette chosen without contrast check.
  6. Fix: Contrast: text 4.5:1 normal and 3:1 for large text (18sp regular or 14sp bold) and UI components/graphics at 3:1 (WCAG AA; confirm against your target version). Adjust tokens in the theme so one change repairs 22 findings; for the orange button, darken the container or use dark text if it reaches ratio:
// theme token fix: derive on-colors from contrast, test with a unit test
fun contrastRatio(a: Color, b: Color): Double {
    val l1 = a.luminance() + 0.05; val l2 = b.luminance() + 0.05
    return maxOf(l1, l2) / minOf(l1, l2)
}
@Test fun brandButtonMeetsAA() = assertTrue(contrastRatio(BrandOrange, OnBrand) >= 4.5)

Fix dialogs in the shared AppDialog (focus trapping, paneTitle, labelled close), labels in shared AppIconButton, then sweep the rest. 7. Prevention: Accessibility in definition of done; CI accessibility checks with baseline; token contrast tests; PR checklist; periodic audits. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not hide problem elements from accessibility to make scanners quiet; that converts a finding into an access barrier.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Brand will not change the orange → Use darker variant for text-bearing surfaces, keep brand orange for non-text accents (3:1 for graphics).
  • Auditor used a different TalkBack version → Reproduce on matching version; semantics are the contract, behavior may differ per version.
  • Can we file waivers? → Only with legal; document the exceptions and a remediation date.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team fixed 87 findings with 11 commits by tracing everything to three components and the color tokens; a CI check later stopped a regression that reintroduced a 2.9:1 gray.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Linear fix list.
  • Hire: Clusters root causes and fixes components.
  • Strong hire: Adds contrast tests, CI gates, priorities by impact and honest trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml: Release 5.12 ships; within 3 days support tickets rise 22%: "Pay button cut off", "cannot see total". Crash rate is flat (0.14%) and no ANRs. Analytics show checkout completion dropping from 61% to 52% in only one cohort: Android 14 users aged 55+ (about 9% of traffic), who commonly set font size to Largest. Layout: bottom bar Row with fixed height(56.dp) containing total Text("Total $1,249.00", maxLines = 1) and a Button. Red herrings: a new payment SDK shipped in the same release; the checkout API p95 rose from 410ms to 480ms.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the payment SDK and latency without segmenting by font scale; "just reduce font size".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the drop correlate with fontScale or display size? Do we log Configuration.fontScale? Does it reproduce on other phones? What changed in the layout this release?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix the bottom bar via remote config/staged rollout; if the layout change is flagged, roll it back.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) fixed height plus maxLines = 1 clipping the total and the button label at 1.5-2.0x font; (b) SDK latency (flat for this cohort? check); (c) API p95 change (affects all users equally, so unlikely to explain a cohort drop).
  4. How I'd verify: Segment funnel by fontScale; reproduce at font scale 2.0 and largest display size on an Android 14 emulator; screenshot tests with @PreviewFontScale-style previews (verify).
  5. Root cause: Layout assumed 1.0 text size. At 200%, 56dp cannot contain a 2-line label plus 16sp padding, and maxLines = 1 ellipsizes the amount; the button's min width is also exceeded in a Row so the label clips.
  6. Fix: Short-term: heightIn(min = 56.dp), remove maxLines = 1 for amount, Modifier.weight for text, wrap the row:
FlowRow(
    Modifier.fillMaxWidth().padding(16.dp),
    horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(12.dp),
    verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(8.dp)
) {
    Text("Total $total", Modifier.weight(1f, fill = true))
    Button(onClick = onPay) { Text("Pay") }
}

(FlowRow is in foundation layout; check the stable status for your version.) Long-term: screenshot tests at font scales 1.0/1.5/2.0 and RTL in CI; avoid fixed heights in design system. 7. Prevention: Log fontScale as a dimension in analytics; QA checklist for large text; a lint check for fixed heights around Text. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not clamp fontScale globally; it hides the issue and violates user settings.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Marketing wants one-line total → Allow wrapping under big font; keep one line at default.
  • Is nonlinear scaling relevant? → On Android 14 large text scales less aggressively, but 2.0 on body text still doubles spaces.
  • Do you also test "Display size"? → Yes: it changes dp width and may trigger narrow layouts.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A funnel dip hid inside a cohort for a week because analytics lacked fontScale; adding it as a dimension turned later layout regressions into a 10-minute diagnosis.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Chases SDK/latency.
  • Hire: Segments by fontScale and fixes clipped layout.
  • Strong hire: Adds CI scale screenshots, analytics dimension and design-system rules.

questions.promptHtml: What does it take to support RTL languages (Arabic, Hebrew) correctly in a Compose and Views app?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Layout direction, icons, and text-input details separate casual from rigorous localization.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Use start/end instead of left/right everywhere, declare android:supportsRtl="true", let Compose resolve LayoutDirection from the locale, mirror directional icons only (back arrows via Icons.AutoMirrored, not logos or media controls), keep numbers, phone numbers and code left-to-right, and test with a pseudo-locale and a real RTL language.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Manifest: android:supportsRtl="true" enables mirroring on API 17+. Views: paddingStart/End, layout_marginStart, textAlignment="viewStart". Compose: Arrangement.Start, PaddingValues(start = ...), Alignment.Start; Modifier.padding(left = ...) does not exist in the same sense for layout-direction-aware APIs; use start/end.
  • LocalLayoutDirection.current gives the direction; CompositionLocalProvider(LocalLayoutDirection provides LayoutDirection.Ltr) forces LTR for content that must not flip (a graph with time on x axis, phone number field).
  • Icons: Material Icons.AutoMirrored.Filled.ArrowBack flips; Modifier.autoMirror or painterResource with android:autoMirrored="true" for vectors.
  • Custom Canvas/drawBehind code uses absolute coordinates; flip manually with layoutDirection.
  • Text: bidirectional text, TextDirection/textDirection for mixed content, BidiFormatter in Views for strings with embedded LTR names; TextAlign.Start rather than Left.
  • Pseudo-locales (ar-XB RTL pseudo, en-XA accent/expansion) catch bugs without translations; translated strings expand 30-40% in German, which also stresses layouts.
  • Pluralization with pluralStringResource; Arabic has 6 plural categories.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Row(horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(8.dp)) {
    Icon(Icons.AutoMirrored.Filled.ArrowBack, contentDescription = stringResource(R.string.back))
    Text(stringResource(R.string.title), textAlign = TextAlign.Start)
}
CompositionLocalProvider(LocalLayoutDirection provides LayoutDirection.Ltr) {
    PhoneNumberField()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Hardcoded Gravity.LEFT or Modifier.offset(x = ...) that ignores direction.
  • Mirroring every icon, including checkmarks, media play, or logos.
  • Concatenating strings ("$a of $b") instead of format resources; word order differs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to test RTL fast? → Developer options "Force RTL layout direction" and pseudo-locale ar-XB.
  2. Gestures such as swipe-back? → Predictive/swipe back direction follows system; custom swipe actions should mirror (swipe direction semantic).
  3. TalkBack in RTL? → Reading order follows layout direction; traversal group indexes are directional-agnostic but swipe right/left semantics reverse.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "use start/end". Senior covers icon mirroring rules, Canvas math, bidi text, forced LTR islands, pseudo-locale testing and plurals.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Middle East launch shipped with a forward arrow pointing the wrong way on every onboarding card and a phone field that reversed digits.

questions.contextHtml: A food delivery app shows an ETA countdown, "Arriving in 12:34", updated every second. After adding liveRegion = LiveRegionMode.Assertive ("so blind users know the ETA"), TalkBack users report the screen is unusable: speech constantly interrupts; they cannot read the order items or reach "Cancel". One-star reviews mention "app talks over itself". Crash rate is 0.1%, normal. Another recent change: the order status text now also has liveRegion. Red herring: a TalkBack update shipped two weeks ago.
questions.promptHtml: What happened, and how do you fix it properly?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch to Polite." Still announces every second, drowning navigation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which element has the live region and how often does its text change? How does the ETA change semantically (each second, or each minute)? Do we have other live regions on screen?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the live region from the ticking node via a hotfix or remote flag.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) per-second text updates with Assertive interrupt TalkBack constantly; (b) additional status live region compounding; (c) TalkBack update changing speech queueing (unlikely cause; the pattern is app-controlled).
  4. How I'd verify: Enable TalkBack and watch the speech queue; log semantics change events; accessibility event logging via adb logcat on TalkBack tag or a debug accessibility service.
  5. Root cause: A live region fires an announcement on every text change; at 1 Hz that is 60 interruptions a minute. Assertive cancels current speech.
  6. Fix: Give the visual countdown no live region and expose a stable, infrequent description: the node's contentDescription as "Arriving in about 13 minutes", updated on minute boundaries; announce meaningful changes only (status transitions, delay greater than 5 minutes) via Polite:
val minutes = remember(etaSeconds) { (etaSeconds + 59) / 60 } // changes once per minute
Text(
    text = formatMmSs(etaSeconds),
    modifier = Modifier.semantics {
        contentDescription = "Arriving in about $minutes minutes"
    }
)
Text(statusText, Modifier.semantics { liveRegion = LiveRegionMode.Polite }) // only on state change

Keep etaSeconds ticking out of recomposition scope of semantics if possible (read in a smaller scope or derive minutes with derivedStateOf). 7. Prevention: Review rule: live region only for events, never for clocks, progress, tickers; a test counting semantics changes over a simulated 60 seconds; QA TalkBack pass on dynamic screens. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not drop all live announcements; important state changes (driver assigned, delayed) still deserve one polite announcement. And I would not use Assertive for non-urgent content.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• User wants exact seconds → They can focus the node and hear the description on demand; announcing proactively is the problem.
  • Does the per-second recomposition hurt too? → Yes if state is read high; read it in a leaf composable or draw/semantic lambda.
  • Haptics or sounds as alternatives? → Possible for urgent events, but respect user settings.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fitness timer screen shipped a spoken per-second countdown and was the single most-cited review complaint among screen reader users until the live region moved to milestone events.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Changes Assertive to Polite only.
  • Hire: Removes per-second announcement, announces events.
  • Strong hire: Separates visual from spoken representation, controls update frequency, adds a test and review rule.
